findings.title: Dynamic imports are started eagerly at module load, so nothing is actually lazy
findings.body: The object literal calls `import("./applecalendar")`, `import("./caldavcalendar")`, … at module evaluation time, which immediately kicks off loading of every app package the moment `@calcom/app-store` is imported. The promises are merely stored, so consumers `await` an already-running import. The net effect is that all ~28 app modules (and their transitive deps such as Stripe/Google/Exchange SDKs) are still evaluated on every request path that touches the app store — the stated goal of async/lazy loading is not achieved, and webpack will still fetch every generated chunk. To get real laziness the entries must be thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, with call sites invoking the thunk.

findings.title: Module-level import promises can produce unhandled rejections and crash the process
findings.body: Each `import("./x")` promise is created at module scope with no attached handler. If any single app module throws while being evaluated (bad/missing app key, failing SDK init, missing optional dependency), the resulting rejection is unhandled because nothing awaits that specific entry unless the app happens to be used. Under Node's default `--unhandled-rejections=throw` this terminates the process, so one broken app takes down the whole server even though no booking uses it. Previously a failing module was at least surfaced synchronously at import time of the specific consumer. Lazily created promises (thunks) or `.catch()` handling is needed.

findings.title: getCalendarCredentials now returns a Promise in its `calendar` field, changing its public contract
findings.body: `getCalendarCredentials` still looks synchronous, but `calendar: getCalendar(credential)` is now a `Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`; any other consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` (it is exported and used outside this module, e.g. destination-calendar/connected-calendar flows and the API app) that calls `item.calendar.listCalendars()` or checks `if (!item.calendar)` will now silently see a truthy Promise and break at runtime. Additionally, promises stored on entries that a caller never awaits can reject unobserved. The function should either be made `async` and resolve the calendars with `Promise.all`, or keep the credential list free of promises.

findings.title: Async callback in forEach: calendar/video cancellations are no longer initiated before the mutation completes
findings.body: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` returns immediately; the deleteEvent/deleteMeeting calls now only start after the `await getCalendar` microtask resolves, i.e. after `requestReschedule` has already sent the reschedule email and possibly returned. Nothing awaits the resulting promises, so failures to delete the old calendar event / video room are swallowed as unhandled rejections and the old events can be left dangling. Use `for (const bookingRef of bookingRefsFiltered) { ... }` with `await`, or collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)`.

findings.title: try/catch around forEach with async callback cannot catch failures anymore
findings.body: Changing the callback to `async` means the surrounding `try { ... } catch { logger.error(...) }` block can never observe an error: the callback returns a promise that is discarded, so any rejection from `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` escapes as an unhandled promise rejection (process-level crash on modern Node) instead of being logged. The deletions are also not awaited before the reschedule email is sent. Replace with a `for...of` loop using `await` inside the try block.

findings.title: try/catch around forEach with async callback cannot catch failures anymore
findings.body: Same problem as in the vital reschedule helper: the callback passed to `forEach` is now `async`, so the enclosing `try/catch` will never see errors thrown inside it; rejections from `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting` become unhandled promise rejections rather than being logged, and the cancellations are not awaited before the function returns. Use a `for...of` loop with `await` inside the try block.

findings.title: Recurring-booking calendar deletions are pushed to apiDeletes after it is already awaited
findings.body: In the recurring branch the credentials are still iterated with `.forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) })`. Because the callback is async, `apiDeletes.push` runs only after the awaits resolve — long after `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at the end of the handler has captured the (still empty) array. So for "cancel all remaining recurring bookings" the external calendar deletions are neither awaited nor error-checked, and failures surface as unhandled rejections. The sibling non-credentialId branch in the same block was correctly converted to a `for...of` loop; this branch should be too.

findings.title: Commented-out example entry points at a non-existent directory
findings.body: The placeholder comment was changed from `// import * as example from "./_example";` to `// example: import("./example"),`. The directory in the repo is `_example`, so a developer who uncomments this line to register a new app gets a module-not-found error. It should read `// example: import("./_example"),`.
